-but I want to impress upon this House that in my judgment if the citizens of Canada are to be as good as we want them to be, adherence to the truth I endeavoured to lay before you in the early part of my address is a very much better, safer and surer road to follow than to enact any compulsory legislation that strives in itself to make a man good when his heart is wrong and he is swearing all the time at being compelled to do a thing he would not do if he followed his own inclination. I do not believe in legislation of that kind. I follow' a Church and a bishop whose doctrines I believe are in close unison and- in conformity with the stand I have now taken. I draw that inference because at a recent gathering the distinguished ecclesiastic in question said we must rely more upon scriptural truths and upon the law of God and the converting power of the salvation of His Son than we must in legislation, enacted sometimes by a majority and some times by a minority, to force people to go in opposition to their will and inclination. The result is, I think, baneful to the law and bad for our owrn faith; it is a case of trusting in our own works to do what the Divine Law alone can do. I put in the same category all these kinds of legislation that seek to force good down a man's throat. I believe in the efficiency of moral suasion and of right doctrines and right beliefs to influence a man, rather than forcing him to be good by legislation.
Perhaps I have said too much in that regard. I now want to commend this Government for some things it has done. I think that the right hon. gentleman who at present leads the House has enumerated enough to show that this Government has done more in great acts of legislation of a far-reaching character than any Canadian Government has done in a like period. It must be remembered that this Government is but a little over two years old, and the recounting of its acts would take a long time. Much of its legislation has been very far-reaching, and much of it has involved hundreds, almost thousands of millions of dollars, and I believe that the future will justify the formation of this legislation.
That is your opinion.
Whether it will be a continuity or not I do not know; it will have to brace up if it is going to carry the country, there is no doubt about that,
Hear, hear.

We on this side will have to get out and talk to the people, because I notice that our friends of the other aggregations are about in the country, and we cannot expect Union principles to flourish while we sit silent in the House of Commons here and allow the other fellows to do all the talking and all the preaching and take all the encomiums for everything that has been done and make the charge that the Government was unwilling to do anything-that it would not have done, what it has done if it had not been forced.
Whether that is the case or not, the Government has so far justified its existence. I agree with the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) in this respect-I shall not discuss the subject now, as I hope to do so on a later occasion-that the economic question will be the next issue upon which the people of this country will be divided at the polls. Whether the member for Nicolet (Mr. Trahan) is justified in believing that Quebec will be just as solid against some other parts of Canada as it was in the last election, I do not know'. It could scarcely be more so than it was at the last election, because on that occasion only three members who sit on this side were elected from the province of Quebec.
I believe that Quebec has considerable light on some questions, and of these the trade question is one. I am sorry that the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is not in his seat, for I should like to ask him whether his removal from Kamouraska to the manufacturing district of Eastern Quebec has had any effect upon his free trade notions. I miss my guess if his views on free trade and protection are not somewhat modified in the near future when they are applied to the good old city of Quebec. Quebec is a manufacturing centre, and Quebec w'ill have something to say about the fiscal question if that is the issue at the next election. And if it is, I for one am quite ready for the fray. On many occasions the people of Canada have expressed a decided opinion upon that question, and if it is put before them again they will give the same answer. I therefore advise the leader of the Opposition to withdraw his amendment and to think it over for a year. If it should

carry and he were sent before the people tomorrow, he would be a disappointed man, because he is not as ready as he thinks he is to face the electorate. I do not wish him any harm so far as his resolution is concerned, but it would be a pity to see him make a failure of his first enterprise in the splendid surroundings of the new Parliament building. I advise him, therefore, to withdraw the amendment; if he does not, it will be ruthlessly slaughtered by the House when the vote is taken upon it.

Mr. Speaker, it is my good luck to have my turn to speak after the honourable member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), for it affords me the opportunity to reply to the question which he had the impertinence to put to the hon. leader of the Opposition, when he asked him what he had done during the war. I hold no brief to defend my leader, as he can well do it himself, but I am anxious to give the member for Brantford the following answerDuring the war, the hon. leader of the Opposition, most conversant with labour questions, was settling some strikes of miners in the United States and was thus working towards bringing closer together employees and employers, thereby enabling munition plants to give their maximum output. The result obtained by the hon. leader of the Opposition, everybody will admit, was a most valuable assistance to the Allies.
But to you, the hon. member for Brantford, might I be allowed to put the same question? What were you doing during the war? You were here in this House and you were supporting, by your vote, all those who were thriving on the sufferings of the people, and permitting certain companies to realize scandalous profits of from 100 to 200 per cent, and you were yourself increasing the prices of agricultural implements of your own manufacture. Such is your patriotism.
I now wish to congratulate the hon. members who have moved and seconded the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. They had to put forth a good deal of willingness and, above all, a lot of imagination in order to find means to praise the present Government, during half an hour respectively, and from that point of view, I do offer them my congratulations.
Every citizen in Canada was eagerly expecting the opening of Parliament. Every one hoped that the Government would at last declare in the speech from the Throne a well defined and settled policy which

would enable the country to emerge from the chaos which the war had wrought, and make it enter upon the road to progress and promotion.
Empty delusion and empty expectation, Mr. Speaker, for this speech gives us no information. Yet, the hon. ministers have repeatedly told us of a reconstruction programme, of an after-war programme which would regenerate the country. What is then the reason of this predicament? It is because the Government have of union but the name; the ministers are at variance and cannot agree upon a programme. The Tory group wants to continue the policy of protection which brings wealth to one class only, whilst the so-called Liberal group is in favour of lowering the tariff, and so, in order to keep themselves in power and avoid appealing to the people, neither group imposes its opinions and the country goes on aimlessly. Those among the ministers who have preserved the sense of Liberalism and who do not want to become hopelessly ruined in the public opinion resign one after another, and the Prime Minister, unable to meet the situation, puts himself on the sick list and travels through unknown lands in order to recuperate.
Mr. Speaker, we have a debt of two billions, we are overburdened with taxes of all kinds, the cost of living is ever increasing, the people are in the power of the Trusts, and meanwhile the Government remain inactive and do nothing to improve the conditions. We are being told again every day that the remedy can be found in economy and overproduction. Economy, Mr. Speaker. Does the Government practise it? Far from it. Every day large amounts are uselessly spent, the ministers launch us into hazardous ventures, such as the purchase of the Canadian Northern, of the Grand Trunk and of the Grand Trunk Pacific; the militia expenses are doubled, fabulous amounts have been spent during the war in order to favour political friends, and now the hon. Minister of Marine informs us of the construction of a navy, after Lord Jellicoe's inspiration, which will imply an expenditure of several million dollars.
Sir, do you not think it would be more in keeping with patriotism to expend those millions towards developing the country, building railroads or building the Georgian Bay canal, a work required for such a long time and which would help developing and enriching the country to such a great extent? Now, what is the Government

doing to encourage overproduction while they so strongly recommend the people to overproduce? Should they not begin by helping the producers? The farmers must be helped,, we must give them the means to produce at low cost by doing away with the duty on all implements required for farming purposes. Sir, I cannot believe that the farmer is obliged to pay one hundred and fifty dollars for a binder which he could secure for seventy-five dollars were the duty abolished. He is forced to enrich the manufacturer, and the consumer is bound to pay a much larger price for the goods which he needs.
Last year, the Government, yielding to public opinion, decided to appoint a certain commission called Board of Commerce. That board was to preclude the manufacturers and the big companies from overcharging the consumer, to preclude them from realizing big profits. But this was a mere allurement, the monopolists and the trusts kept forestalling all the products and piling them up in the warehouses so as to increase the prices, and the chairman of that board has just handed the Government his resignation out of disgust, saying that the law was ineffective and his hands were tied up by political influences. That is, Sir, what the Government has done to reduce the cost of living.
It is said, in the speech from the Throne, that a new Franchise Act will be brought down. I am glad of it. I am delighted to hear that the iniquitous War-time Elections Act will be struck off our statute book forever. I ask the Government to give us a Franchise Act fair and just and allowing the people to speak out freely. Let everybody be enfranchised. In a democratic country as Canada is, every citizen, whether rich or poor, whether big or small, should have the right to say what he thinks of the public men and of the political questions. The right to vote is a sacred advantage which should be enjoyed by the workingman and by the manufacturer alike, by the mechanic as well as by the farmer. Though wishing to make no prediction, 1 feel assured that if we are given a Franchise Act in keeping with ever so little honesty, of those who are now sitting to our right, Sir, not excepting even the honourable ministers, very few will come back to Parliament after the next general election.
I see it is also proposed to amend the law with respect to labour. That is most serious at this moment, Mr. Speaker. You are fully aware of all the uneasiness which
now prevails between capital and labour, of all the strikes which have taken place throughout the country. As I have said it in this House on a previous occasion, as a matter of principle, I am not in favour of strikes,, but I think that the workingmen are not entirely wrong, they suffered from the war to a greater extent than any other class, and now that the war is over, they suffer from the high cost of living to a greater extent than any other class also; and while they are toiling and enduring all kinds of hardships, the Government allows the manufacturers and the millionaires to double the amount of their fortunes. Is there, in this country, a single citizen who will claim that the workingman was properly treated by the Government? Let us better his position, let us secure for him better protection against accidents and in case he is out of work; in fine, iSi.r, let us grant him an old age pension. While not wishing in any way to worry the House, I would again repeat my request: It is my earnest belief that when a workingman has kept toiling all his life and, in many cases for a salary which was inadequate, to enrich his employer, who decides to dispense with his services when he has become old and incapacitated, should be protected by the State to the extent of being relieved of the alternative of remaining a burden to his children or of being obliged to take the road to the hospital. I know that this request of mine will not be favourably considered, for the Government is now dismissing humdrreds of employees at the Printing Bureau, under the pretence that they are too old. Such a course is shameful and I protest against such dismissals of old servants.
Mr. Speaker, I have fully appreciated the sympathetic remarks made by the Acting Prime Minister about the French Canadians, the other day; we have been so little accustomed to such flattering compliments, for a few years past especially, that we cannot believe what we hear. Though believing the hon. minister to be in good faith, I may tell him that it will take more than words to make us forget the abuse and the sufferings which we had to endure. He must give us our full share of representation in the Government, the commissions and all public appointments.
Of late years, this Government's policy has favoured the complete exclusion of French Canadians from public service. Today, you praise the the province of Quebec; you find that our citizens are peaceful and

clear-sighted. It is a fact Mr. Speaker. The best indication in this connection is the peace and tranquility which have prevailed in our province since the war is ended, while unrest and strikes are rampant in all the other provinces of the Dominion. What is the reason for this, Mr. Speaker? It is because my fellow-countrymen are imbued with the spirit of Catholicism and accept the guidance of the Catholic Church which teaches the people to respect and obey all laws.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I urge the Government and all the bon. members to support the amendment moved by the hon. leader of the Opposition asking for an immediate election. A few days ago, I heard the Acting Prime Minister state here that the members of the Opposition were not in earnest and would find themselves in a sad plight if the writs were issued for a general election. Well, then why not accept our challenge, Mr. Minister? Dissolve Parliament and let us go before the electorate. For my part, I am confident of what the outcome will be. I remember that in 1896, the country was getting through a period of depression pretty similar to the one whose effects are being felt to-day. The Canadian people turned their eyes towards the Liberal party then under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. There followed a period of fifteen years of wise and progressive administration. Today as in 1896, the people of Canada turn their eyes toward the Liberal party which is under the direction of a new leader, young and talented, in whom we have placed all our hopes and who will also be able to give to this country of ours a prudent and progressive government.

gain the support of the members of the Cabinet, he will let them have their way. If he is a weak man he will let them have their way, perhaps for more ignoble reasons. The consequence is that Parliament is the one and only means of effectively controlling expenditure. That brings me to a consideration of the method of voting estimates. There is not a member of this House, I am sure, who has not felt the futility of our method. When the estimates are submitted to Parliament some member, on the Opposition side generally, and once in a while, under present circumstances, a member on this side of the House arises and makes a few remarks perhaps about some steamboat that has been taken off its usual course, or wants to know why some clerk has been dismissed. Sometimes these matters take up three or four hours, and finally the estimates go through in bulk, because that has been the practice for the last thirty or forty or fifty years. That is the degree of attention that Parliament gives the estimates. No man can possibly make himself familiar with all the estimates; indeed, it is pretty nearly a life work to make oneself familiar enough with one department to discuss its estimates effectively. How can we remedy this? Let us see what the Mother of Parliaments has done in order to get control over expenditures. In 1912 the British House appointed a committee on estimates. It acted through one session, and it was found that it could deal during the session with practically only one department. It was an ordinary committee of the House, without any clerical assistance, and had to do all its work within the session, and it was going to take thirty or forty years to scrutinize all the estimates. It could not get the necessary information on all the estimates and make a report in time for the House to deal with them that session, and consequently, when the war came, that committee was dropped. The next time you come across a reference to it is in the seventh and ninth report of the 8elect Committee on National Expenditure of 1917, of which the Hon. Herbert Samuel was chairman. The whole question was dealt with by that committee, and better means were devised for controlling the expenditure, which means I commend to the consideration of this House. The Committee, it was proposed, should have an officer known as The Examiner of Estimates," as well as a clerical staff acting under the direction of the committee. The committee was composed of thirty members, I believe, divided 
into two sections, one section dealing with the main estimates, and the other with estimates for new undertakings, or what we would call subliminary estimates. There were two recommendations which must be considered if the project is to be successful. One of these is that the estimates as published should be more significant and that their allocation should be by objects rathrr than by subjects. The other recommendation was that a vote for reducing an estimate should not be regarded as'a want of confidence motion. If it is made a want of confidence motion, the judgment of the House is no longer economic, but political. The Government supporters are not going to turn out the Government because they differ with them on the expenditure of $10.000 or $50,000 or $100,000. There may be cases where the Government would be justified in asking their supporters to pass a particular estimate, but in the main a motion to reduce an estimate should not ia regarded as a want of confidence motion. I commend to the House the serious study of that means of retrenchment. It is the only one that will furnish the House with the machinery whereby we can attain the retrenchment that is going to be necessary in the immediate months. I should like to see this House appoint a committee on estimates this year. At the very least, I would ask that a committee be appointed to consider the matter and leport to the House. One or two things have struck me in considering this matter. I think the House has been rather slack of recent years in its understanding of financial principles. Certain Bills have been passed providing for an expenditure of money over a series of years. For instance, the Highways Bill provides for an annual grant for the next five or ten years. The same is true with regard to The Agricultural Aid and Technical Education Grants. Now that system practically takes out of Parliament's hands the control over expenditure. It is a wrong principle, and the instance serves to demonstrate the need for more attention and greater care by this House in the passing of financial measures. We have got away from the old ideas which have brought us to where we stand to-day, the fear of the encroachment of autocracy, the fear, perhaps, even of an aristocracy. We are fully democratic today, but still we sometimes forget the sound principles which we worked out in conflict, and I take it, that is true in this particular case.

There are other matters in this connection which I think require the attention of the House. I cannot see, for instance, why in the present condition of exchange our Customs Department should not enter imported goods from the United States and England at their Canadian value instead of at the United States or English value. I understand that what our Customs Department is doing to-day is this: You buy, we will suppose, $1,170 of goods in the United States. Owing to the rate of exchange, these goods are valued in the United States at $1,000, and they are entered by our Customs Department at $1,000, and on that the customs tax is levied. On the other hand, when you buy $700 of goods from Great Britain, you get $972 worth of goods in sterling. When the goods enter this country they are valued at $972, and the consequence is that our British preference is wiped out by our application of the customs tax. The application is wrong, because when the exchange is running in our favour, as it is with Great Britain, it encouiages exports to us from Britain, and when it is running against us, as it is with the United States, it discourages exports to us from the United States.
How far has the principle of protection been applied in this matter to decide the way in which we should treat the money value of the goods? I take it that this is a matter about which the people of Canada are very greatly concerned. It is contrary to sound principle that we should take the goods at other than our own value. If a man can buy $970 worth of goods in Great Britain for $700, he should have the advantage of his purchase, and I do not think the manufacturers of Canada have any right to say that he should not. I fear, therefore, that on that question our Government has made a concession which is a betrayal of principal. We should also give some attention to the Excess Profits Tax. The fact that a man may take out of 1919 earnings the tax he paid in 1918 is surely one way of adding his taxes to the cost of doing business. It enables him to escape taxation and tranfer the burden to the consumers. I have a very grave doubt as to the soundness of the principle of our Excess Profits Tax, nevertheless, while it is in operation it should be properly applied. I mention the matter now, however, by way of criticism. It seems to me that the Opposition are not the people who have been criticising the Government. Rather it has been the friends of the Government, as far as I have
observed since I have been in the House. It seems to me that the matters of practical import and great consequence are suggested by the friends of the Government, -things that should really be done. A good deal of nonsense is talked about politics and the struggle between Ontario and Quebec, and I think we had better relegate to the region of oblivion all questions of the past. They are dead; and as we are faced with present problems which are serious enough I think more of us should get in on the Forward Movement and look to the future.
I should like to say a few words in regard to the question of co-operation. I observe that Judge Robson in his report the other day said that incidentally, and I am sure by oversight, there was in the Combines and Fair Prices Act an obstruction upon the principle of co-operation, and that it was not allowed scope for development. I believe that consumers' co-operation, and growing out of that, probably, producers' co-operation, will prove to be one of the solutions of our present industrial difficulties. There is no doubt that consumers' cooperation will be a regulator of prices as it has been in Great Britain. At present we have nothing but the industrial system and the production of goods for profit. Much criticism has been levelled at the doctrine that business should be carried on for use and not for profit. I have seen but one place where there has been a really practical application of that principle, and that is in connection with the co-operative movement in Great Britain. There profits are distributed in accordance with the amount of purchases, and prices are governed. Out of the retail societies, of which there are nearly fourteen hundred, wholesale cooperatives have been formed and these have started factories, which produce goods only for the use of the retail dealers who are their customers, and are co-operators with them. The fact that you have a large part of industry carried on under co-operation is more or less an index of needs to the remainder of the trade, and it is undoubtedly a governing influence as to prices and what are fair profits and fair dividends. The man who becomes a co-operator very soon comes to understand the use and value of investments. He has an interest in the present system, and is not apt to become a socialist or communist. He has property and understands its value and knows how it can be made to improve his position. In this House the late Mr. Monk, I understand, in 1907 endeavoured unsuccessfully to have enacted a Bill permitting the formation of
no

co-operative societies. I happened to be on the Cost of Living Committee last year, and we came face to face with the fact that the trade of Canada has its face set like adamant against co-operation. From the manufacturer down to the retail dealer there is no use for co-operation, and this House must therefore open the way by proper legislation for the formation of co-operative societies, and give them the opportunity they enjoy in Great Britain. To illustrate what is being done in Great Britain, I may say that the customers number ten millions of people, and there is a membership of two and a half millions. When recently, in connection with the establishment of a Board of Commerce similar to our own, the President of the Board of Trade was about to make appointments, he chose first a chairman, who from a slate, which was prepared by the President of the Board of Trade, selected from amongst the cooperators and trades unions, the men who should be associated with him on the board. Now, what greater recognition could there be of the sound democratic and public-service position to which co-operation had attained in Great Britain than that recognition by the Government of the United Kingdom?

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks on the Address, I desire at the outset to discharge the pleasant duty of paying tribute to the mover and seconder for the splendid way in which they acquitted themselves in their task. Their speeches were unquestionably excellent examples of oratory, and the sentiments which they expressed were on the whole admirable. I trust that we shall have many sifch academic treats as those with which we were favoured on that occasion. I congratulate the seconder of the Address, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McGregor), whose debut in this House certainly must commend him to the attention of his electors as well as of his province and the Dominion. As a business man might be expected to do, he gave a practical address, submitting figures which gave food for thought. I am sure that his electors have been reading his speech with delight.
It had been my intention also a few moments ago when I decided to address this House to extend some congratulations, which I believed were well deserved, to my right hon. friend the acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster). My intention was to have given him my due and sincere eon-

gratulations upon the most eloquent speech that he delivered on the day of the opening of the House in the language of Racine, Boileau and Fenelon. His remarks were such as to commend them to the attention of every one who speaks the French language and who appreciates the nobility and beauty of that tongue. I was aware, as were others, that the right hon. gentleman could write the language with correctness and could use it when circumstances required that he should do so, but I was surprised and delighted with the facility with which he expressed himself on that occasion in language which was not a mere translation of English expressions but language which a Frenchman would have used had he been speaking under similar circumstances. I wish to congratulate him not only upon his ability to speak the French language with facility and lucidity but also because he has given an example to the whole of Canada that the French language is one of the dual languages of Confederation and which had the same official recognition as English throughout the Dominion. A few days ago in the city of Ottawa the Educational Conference declared that the French language was necessary in the future not only for the happiness and intellectual enjoyment of the people of Canada, but for the advancement of economic and social conditions. It was my good fortune four or five years ago to tell my compatriots in the city of Ottawa that under the British flag the French language was bound to get recognition and that in a few years that language would be on an equal footing with the languages of other countries. I see that to-day there is a tendency to give full justice to the French language in Canada, as it is being recognized that a wider knowledge of that language must contribute to the greater felicity and prosperity of the Canadian people. I hope my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) will kindly convey my remarks and congratulations to his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if I have, in the exercise of my duty, given due credit to the right hon. the Acting Prime Minister, I deem it also my duty to call his attention to another subject upon which I am not able to felicitate or congratulate him; that is the absence of a Cabinet minister representing the province of New Brunswick for the last ten or eleven months, and, indeed, the absence of a Cabinet representative from all of the eastern provinces, including Nova Scotia. We see that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), who

represents that province, is not able to discharge the duties of his office. Personally, I need not say that if my good wishes' could restore the Prime Minister to health he would certainly come back full of vigour to resume his official duties. But the eastern provinces have no .representative in the Government-those eastern provinces which have been the backbone of Confederation, without which there could have been no Confederation-and it is the duty of the Government not to prolong such a state of affairs. We are told, and we can see, that the only reason why the Maritime Provinces are unrepresented is that if there were a byelection in New Brunswick the people would not be found to be very favourable to the Government. We cannot wait, until a new census is taken, as the Iron, member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis) has suggested, to have representation in the Government from the province of New Brunswick. If for that reason a by-election would not be agreeable, then, I say, let us have a general election. When the Liberal party come back to power we will be able to have by-elections and we will have representatives from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and the French elements of the province of Quebec. That was the main reason why I rose to-day to give my support to the amendment brought in by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Air. Mackenzie King). In a speech which will long remain in the memory when it has been read, pondered and cogitated over by the people of Canada, the leader of the Opposition claimed that it was time for an election, that the Government were not here representing the aspirations of the people of Canada, were not here fulfilling the promises that were made to the people, and were not here for the purpose for which they had been elected. They were placed here as a Union Government for the duration of the war, but now that the war was over the people should be permitted, in the exercise of their right, to select another Government which would be representative of the opinion of the people as it would find expression to-day.
My" hon. friend from Neepawa has said that a census will be taken in two or three years and that we must wait until the census is taken in order to give the West the representation to which it will have a right at that time. No one has more consideration for the constitution of Canada than I. At the same time, speaking more particularly as I do for the eastern provinces and for the farming interest, the basic industry
of Canada, which is waiting to-day for some relief and some encouragement in its work, which has been clamouring for the last two or three years for a reduction of the tariff, more particularly on food products and the material necessary for carrying on its operations, I assert that the time has come to again consult the people of Canada. Having voted for our amendment last year, are these hon. gentlemen, among whom was the hon. member for Neepawa, going to say to-day: "We are willing to allow the Government to stand by the high protectionist tariff; we will put away our principles and our aspirations and wait for two or three years until the Government has taken the census and provided for a redistribution of seats in this country?"
If the policy of reciprocity for -which the West voted almost unanimously-a policy under which the farmers' wheat and other cereals and live stock would have found a ready market in the United States, and -which would have resulted in great prosperity in Canada as a whole-had been adopted in 1911 would it not have prevented much of the unrest wdiieh exists throughout the country to-day? Had' that policy, which was so generally approved by the farmers in Alberta, Saskatchewan and a good part of Manitoba, gone into effect should we have seen as we do to-day the farmers of the West organizing in the manner in which they are in order to secure the passage of legislation better calculated to advance their interests? I must say that I sympathize with the movement because I have been for many years in my own constituency, closely identified with the great industry of agriculture to say nothing of the sister industry of fishing, and I have been very loyally supported for the past twenty years by the farmers and fishermen there. I am confident that they are prepared to continue that support for a like period of time because they know how warmly I am devoted to their interests. Why wait for two or three years until we have' another census and a re-distribution of seats when that means the continuance of the policy of protection and the perpetuation of the existing dissatisfaction? Does my hon. friend from Neepawa under the existing circumstances expect to see any immediate reduction of the tariff, is he hopeful of securing free trade to the extent that is practicable, in view of the recent pronouncements of members of the Government, especially the deliverance of my intellectual and genial friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen)? In my opin-

ion the farmers will not see any free-trade policy adopted or very much in the way of reduction of the tariff or of taxation. We are told that the maintenance of a tariff is necessary in order to meet our yearly ordinary expenditures of some $150,000,000, the $35,000,000 to $40,000,000 of pensions to our soldiers, and other obligations. We are told that we must depend upon the tariff to meet obligations which would seem fabulous were it not that the public mind since the war has grown accustomed to think in millions. But the tariff is not the only source of revenue. The taxation of land values has been strongly urged and my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has been one of its strongest advocates. If the taxation of land values is a good policy to pursue it should have been adopted long before this. But even now why not put it into operation and thus raise the augmented revenues we so greatly need for our public demands? If I recollect aright the hon. gentleman (Mr. *Crerar) speaking to this House last year estimated that a revenue of seventy-five or eighty million dollars could be derived from the -taxation of land values. Why refrain from having recourse to this tax, especially at this time when the farmers are straining every effort to meet their necessities under the present high cost of living and the high rate of farm labour?
When we ask for an appeal to the people we are told to wait until there is another census and until there has been a re-distribution of seats. It is frequently stated, and some hon. gentlemen opposite as well as the newspapers supporting them take pleasure in repeating the statement, that the Liberals are not sincere in asking for a general election. Well, Mr. Speaker, you have known me for some years and you will admit that I do not make a statement which I do not believe or give expression to a hope which I do not sincerely entertain. I am of the opinion that the time has come when the Government, oi its own volition, should appeal to the country. If the present Government should be returned well and good, but the people will not be satisfied until they have had an opportunity of expressing their will at the polls, because it cannot be denied that under the conditions which prevail this Government is not a constitutional Government.
The present state of exchange between Canada and the United States, in my opinion, is iesponsible for a great deal of dissatisfaction in the public mind. For this

condition a great many people blame the United States but does the responsibility rest with that country? Undoubtedly that exchange rate is a matter for concern. It has been urged that the Minister of Finance, (Sir Henry Drayton) for whose financial and legal ability I have the greatest respect, should take steps to secure relief. I do not altogether agree with what has so far been done in that direction. We have been told that we should buy less from the United States and produce more, but in my opinion had the Liberal trade policy of 1911 been carried into effect we should have seen to-day a greater equilibrium in the figures of trade with our neighbours to the south, our exports would have been more on a parity with our imports from that country and eminent financiers of the United States would have had a more exalted opinion of our currency. Gold is the basis of currency in the United States, whereas we might say that Canadian currency is on a paper basis. As a remedial measure our Minister of Finance recently exported some $40,000,000 in gold to the United States. To my mind it would have been much better to have stored that gold in the vaults of Canada and issued against it a proportional amount of paper currency redeemable in gold. Had these measures, which I have urged, been followed I believe that to-day our currency would have-been on a basis equally as satisfactory as that of the United States. I suggest that as much gold as can be got together be put in the vaults of Canada in order that the value of our paper currency may be increased and put on an equal footing with that of United States.
When we vote for the amendment which has been submitted by the leader of the Opposition we do so in the hope that the members of the Government will be led to carry out the constitutional duties involving upon them; that they will pass a Franchise Act which is in accordance with the British practice and the British spirit, giving every Canadian who is entitled to vote the right to the franchise, and then go before the people.
It has been said by some hon. gentleman that party government no longer exists in Canada. The member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) suggested yesterday that if hon. gentlemen opposite who were supporting the Union Government should make themselves a party, they would keep themselves in power. But whatever may be done in that respect I hope that when the Minister of Finance brings down his Budget there

will be found in it some departure from the old ways of the Tory administration, from the old practice of keeping to the same source of revenue-Tariff, and more tariff.
I believe that hon. gentlemen who are supporting the cause of the farmers in this House are in sympathy with our programme. The programme of the farmers and the programme of the Liberal party are, in a sense, but one; there is no considerable difference between them. Whatever is embodied in either may easily be embodied in the other without any great violation of principle.

In the event of an election taking place immediately without redistribution, how long will the farmers of the West have to wait before the Government which my hon. friend boasts would come into power would bring about a redistribution of the representation in Parliament?

It has been the practice of the Liberal party-particularly was it so during the leadership of the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier-to appeal to the people at frequent intervals. In order to give the country the benefit of the reciprocity agreement of 1911-
Will the hon. gen-* tleman permit me? I put a question to him.
Let him finish his answer.

I was proceeding to answer my hon. friend; if he is in a hurry I will speak as rapidly as I can. I was saying that when questions of vital interest to the people have been at issue the Liberal party has always been willing, even after so short a period as a year or six months in office, again to go before the country and submit their policies to the people. In 1911, three years after an election had been held, the then Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when the reciprocity agreement was brought forward and objection was made to it by the Opposition, might quite properly have let the agreement stand and remained in power for another two years. But in the interests of the people he immediately dissolved Parliament and went to the country. That principle will always be followed by the Liberal party; we are always ready to appeal to the people whenever occasion requires. It is only members on the other side who are talking about prolonging the present Parliament.
We would be well advised, therefore, to persuade the members of the Government 8
that they are certainly holding a false position. The purpose for which the Government was elected has been fulfilled, and they should now appeal to the people. The ministers might not all be defeated, but certainly there will be a great change after the next election, in Ontario as well as throughout the West. The farmers all over the country are agitating for a change, and whoever may make up the new Government I am willing to accept the verdict of the people. The desire of the Liberal party is not so much to attain power as to uphold the principles which it endorses and which it wishes to be enjoyed by the people of Canada. Our object is to promote the in-ierests of the Canadian people; whether we do that in Opposition or otherwise is not the most important matter. In the past the Liberal party have done great things for Canada, not only by preventing the adoption of measures which would not have been good for our country, but also by assisting in the enactment of legislation which, but for our labours, might not have been so beneficial.
I hope that the Government will bring down a Franchise Act which will give the franchise to every Canadian, every British subject in this country who has a vote, whatever his political views may be. The people have been asking for a proper Franchise Act ever since the last election-an election which certainly was no credit to the party which obtained the majority of the votes; an election in which neither the civilian population nor the soldiers were allowed to enjoy the full privileges of the franchise.
Therefore, with all this unrest in the minds of the people, the Government should hasten to bring down a fair and equitable Franchise Act, and also to bring down whatever appropriations may be required for carrying on the affairs of the country. Then let them appeal to the people, and if it be the will of the people to return them to power, we are prepared to abide by the result, although I do not believe that they will be returned to power. We want a just franchise with the British spirit in it. We want it to be just for everybody, for the man of the West as well as for the man of the East; we want it to be just for the man who came here ten, fifteen or twenty years ago under the promise of receiving the advantages of British freedom and British institutions, for the maintenance and preservation of which in Canada as in other parts of the British Empire our sons have fought and died. British principles and institutions form a large part



of our constitution. Therefore, let the franchise be in accordance with those principles, and more particularly in accordance with those sentiments which are conveyed in the term "British spirit," which means freedom in every possible way and justice to all. I trust that the Government will see fit to give us such a franchise.
